Alan Mathison Turing (1912–1954) was a talented British mathematician and logician whose work laid the foundation for modern computer science and artificial intelligence. He made significant contributions to the field of cryptography and codebreaking in World War II, and was instrumental in breaking Nazi communication encryptions. Near the end of his life, he was convicted of homosexuality and was subsequently chemically castrated. In 1936, Turing published a paper that is now recognised as the foundation of computer science. Turing analysed what it meant for a human to follow a definite method or procedure to perform a task. For this purpose, he invented the idea of a ‘Universal Machine’ that could decode and perform any set of instructions. Ten years later he would turn this revolutionary idea into a practical plan for an electronic computer, capable of running any program. [...] Now he focused on the use of computers. plan.title: Alan Turing: The Man Who Imagined Modern Computers
plan.description: Alan Turing was a British mathematician whose 1936 idea of a universal machine laid the foundation for computer science. He also helped break Enigma at Bletchley Park and posed the question behind the Turing test.

beats.narration: In 1950, a British mathematician asked a question that still shapes our world: can a machine think? His name was Alan Turing, and he had already changed history once.
Turing was born in London in 1912. He was often a lonely child, fostered in English homes while his parents lived in India. Numbers and logic became his refuge.
His brilliance showed early. At Cambridge he studied mathematics, and in 1936 he published the paper that is now recognised as the foundation of computer science.
Born in London in 1912. Fellow at King's College at just twenty-two. Then a PhD from Princeton in 1938.
His big idea was a universal machine. It could follow any set of instructions you gave it. That single concept underpins every computer, phone and laptop we use today.
Then came the Second World War. Turing worked at Bletchley Park, Britain's top-secret codebreaking centre, and played a pivotal role in decrypting German messages protected by the Enigma code.
After the war, he turned his mind to building electronic computers, and to brains. In 1948 he described what may be the first learning neural network, but his manuscript was rejected.

beats.narration: In 1950 he proposed the imitation game, now called the Turing test. If you cannot tell machine from human by conversation, he asked, why not call it thinking?

props.text: Can a machine's answers be told apart from a human's?

beats.narration: Britain repaid him cruelly. Turing was convicted of homosexuality and subjected to chemical castration. He died in 1954, aged forty-one. A royal pardon came some sixty years later.
Today his ideas run through every screen and every talking machine. Turing asked whether machines could think, and the world is still answering him.

accuracy.reason: Mostly matches the notes, but "Fellow at King's College at just twenty-two" is dated 1934 on the timeline, while he was elected in 1935. The Enigma claim is vague, and the 1952 conviction and 2013 pardon are left out. The claim "every computer, phone and laptop" is overstated.

coverage.reason: Covers the universal machine, Bletchley, the Turing test, the conviction and the pardon. Enigma gets only one sentence, and there is no mention of the bombe or of his role in shortening the war. The 1952 date and the 2013 pardon year are missing, and the early life gets too much time.

structure.reason: The order is chronological with chapters and a closing callback to the opening question. Beats 2–4 repeat the birth and the early biography.

hook_ending.reason: The opening question about a machine thinking is a good hook. The ending returns to that question, though it is somewhat conventional.

tone.reason: Respectful and accessible. "Britain repaid him cruelly" is a little dramatic but fitting.
